term: Defender XDR unified incident queue
def: Microsoft Defender XDR automatically correlates related alerts from Defender for Endpoint, Defender for Office 365, Defender for Identity, and Defender for Cloud Apps into a single incident, so an analyst investigates one correlated case instead of chasing separate alerts from each product individually.
eg: Because Sentinel can sync bidirectionally with Defender XDR incidents, the same correlated incident can also be worked from the Sentinel incident queue, keeping status and assignment consistent across both portals.

term: Automated investigation and response (AIR) in Defender XDR
def: AIR automatically investigates alerts using the same playbooks a human analyst would follow, then either remediates the threat directly or produces pending actions in the Action Center for an analyst to approve, depending on the configured automation level.
prompt: _____ automatically investigates alerts using the same playbooks a human analyst would follow, then either remediates the threat directly or produces pending actions in the Action Center for an analyst to approve, depending on the configured automation level.
eg: Automation level 'Full - remediate threats automatically' takes action without waiting for approval, while 'Semi - require approval for any remediation' (or for non-temp/core folders) leaves every remediation as a pending action until an analyst reviews it.

term: Sentinel automation rules vs. playbooks
def: An automation rule is the lightweight, no-code layer that decides what happens when an incident is created or updated, or an alert is created, in Sentinel -- assigning an owner, changing severity, adding a tag, closing as a false positive, or running one or more playbooks. A playbook is a Logic App that does the actual work, such as calling an API, isolating a device, or posting to Teams.
eg: Automation rules can also control the order multiple rules run in and can suppress lower-priority rules from running once a higher-priority one has already handled the incident.

term: Playbook triggers: incident trigger vs. alert trigger
def: A Sentinel playbook built on the Microsoft Sentinel incident trigger runs against a whole incident (with all its correlated alerts and entities), while one built on the alert trigger runs against a single alert. An automation rule can run only playbooks that start with the same trigger as the rule itself: incident-trigger playbooks for incident-created or incident-updated rules, and alert-trigger playbooks for rules on the 'When alert is created' trigger. Attaching an alert-trigger playbook directly inside an analytics rule was the older classic method, which Microsoft retired in March 2026.
eg: Building new playbooks on the incident trigger is the current recommended approach, since it lets the playbook act on the full incident context rather than just one contributing alert.

term: Sentinel analytics rule types: scheduled, NRT, and Fusion
def: A scheduled analytics rule runs a KQL query on a defined interval and lookback period, generating an incident on matches. A near-real-time (NRT) rule runs about every minute against a narrower set of supported tables for faster detection. Fusion correlates multiple lower-fidelity anomalies from different sources into one higher-confidence incident using machine learning, without an analyst writing any KQL for it.
eg: NRT rules trade query flexibility for speed -- only a limited set of tables and functions are supported -- so they are reserved for detections where the extra latency of a scheduled rule genuinely matters.

term: Custom log tables and Data Collection Rules (DCRs)
def: Ingesting a custom log source into Sentinel's Log Analytics workspace defines a custom table (suffixed _CL) whose schema and any ingestion-time transformation are controlled by a Data Collection Rule, which can filter, parse, or reshape the incoming data before it is stored and billed.
eg: Because a DCR transformation runs at ingestion time, dropping unneeded columns or noisy rows there reduces both storage cost and the volume an analytics rule or hunting query later has to scan.

term: MITRE ATT&CK coverage in Sentinel
def: Sentinel tags analytics rules with the MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques they detect, and the MITRE ATT&CK workbook/blade visualizes which techniques have active coverage, which have coverage only from a currently disabled rule, and which have none at all.
eg: A gap showing 'no coverage' for a technique relevant to the organization's threat model is exactly what drives which analytics rule template to enable next, rather than enabling rules at random from the content hub.

term: Microsoft Security Copilot in the SOC workflow
def: Security Copilot is a generative-AI assistant embedded in Sentinel and Defender XDR that can summarize an incident in plain language, suggest or generate a KQL query from a natural-language prompt, reverse-engineer a suspicious script, and draft an incident report, all grounded in the organization's own connected security data.
eg: Copilot accelerates triage and hunting by drafting a starting KQL query or explaining an unfamiliar entity, but an analyst still reviews and validates its output before acting on it, the same as any other analyst-authored finding. Security Copilot also runs agents (triage, threat intelligence briefing, analysis, dynamic detection) that use SCUs, and is included for eligible Microsoft 365 E5 and E7 customers.

term: Watchlists in Microsoft Sentinel
def: A watchlist is analyst-curated reference data (imported from a CSV, like a list of VIP users, terminated employees, or known-good IP ranges) that can be joined against log data in analytics rules and hunting queries using the _GetWatchlist() function.
eg: Joining an analytics rule query against a terminated-employees watchlist can turn an otherwise-routine sign-in event into a high-priority incident purely because of who the account belongs to.

term: User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) in Sentinel
def: UEBA builds a behavioral baseline per user and entity from signals across connected data sources, then surfaces anomalies (like a sign-in from an unusual location or access to a resource the user has never touched before) as enrichment on investigations, independent of whether any single analytics rule fired.
prompt: _____ builds a behavioral baseline per user and entity from signals across connected data sources, then surfaces anomalies (like a sign-in from an unusual location or access to a resource the user has never touched before) as enrichment on investigations, independent of whether any single analytics rule fired.
eg: UEBA's value is catching activity that looks individually unremarkable but is anomalous specifically for that entity's own history, which a static threshold-based analytics rule would not flag.

term: Content hub and Sentinel solutions
def: The content hub is where an analyst installs a packaged solution (bundling data connectors, analytics rule templates, workbooks, hunting queries, and playbooks) for a specific product or scenario, such as a solution for Microsoft Entra ID or a specific third-party firewall.
eg: Installing a solution only stages its analytics rule templates for review; each template must still be explicitly enabled (and often tuned) before it starts generating incidents.

term: Analytics rule tuning: entity mapping and alert grouping
def: Entity mapping tells Sentinel which query columns represent entities like Account, Host, or IP, which drives incident correlation, entity-page enrichment, and UEBA. Alert grouping settings control whether multiple alerts from the same rule within a time window are combined into one incident or create separate incidents.
eg: Without correct entity mapping, two related alerts that both involve the same compromised account may fail to correlate into a single incident even when the underlying analytics rule fired correctly on each one.

term: Alert suppression vs. excluding an entity from an analytics rule
def: Alert suppression is a setting on an analytics rule that stops the rule from running its query for a defined period after it generates an alert, which silences it for every source. Explicitly excluding a known-noisy entity (like a scanner's IP address) inside the analytics rule query itself prevents just that source from ever matching, without silencing the rule for everyone else.
eg: Suppression is a temporary, rule-wide snooze; editing the query to exclude a specific entity is a permanent, source-scoped tuning change -- a false-positive review usually calls for the second, not the first.

term: Threat intelligence indicators in Sentinel
def: Threat intelligence indicators (IPs, domains, file hashes, URLs) can be ingested from Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence, TAXII feeds, or the upload API/UI, stored in the ThreatIntelIndicators and ThreatIntelObjects tables (which replaced the legacy ThreatIntelligenceIndicator table, which stopped receiving data after July 31, 2025), and matched against log data automatically by the built-in TI-based analytics rule templates.
eg: A hunting query can also join directly against the threat intelligence tables to check historical log data for any past match against a newly learned indicator, not only future activity going forward.

term: Automation rule ordering and incident triggers
def: Multiple automation rules scoped to the same analytics rule run in a defined order (lowest number first), and an earlier rule's actions can change what a later rule sees -- for example, closing the incident as a false positive -- which is why rule order matters when an auto-close rule needs to act before a notification or playbook rule would otherwise run.
eg: A common misconfiguration is a broad 'assign and notify' automation rule running before a narrower 'auto-close known-benign pattern' rule, which wastes a notification and an assignment on an incident that was always going to be closed automatically anyway.

term: Sentinel workbooks for operational visibility
def: A workbook is an interactive report built from KQL queries against the workspace, used to visualize trends like incident volume by severity, analytics rule health, data connector ingestion latency, or SOC operational metrics like mean time to triage.
eg: Workbooks are for humans to read trends and spot drift over time; they do not themselves generate incidents or take remediation action the way an analytics rule or playbook does.

term: Log Analytics workspace
def: The underlying Azure Monitor data store that Microsoft Sentinel is built on top of — every ingested log, custom table, and Data Collection Rule ultimately lands in a Log Analytics workspace, which is what KQL queries actually run against.
prompt: The underlying Azure Monitor data store that Microsoft Sentinel is built on top of — every ingested log, custom table, and Data Collection Rule ultimately lands in a _____, which is what KQL queries actually run against.
eg: Enabling Sentinel doesn't create a separate data store — it activates Sentinel's analytics and case-management layer on top of a Log Analytics workspace you choose (or create).

term: Sentinel data connectors
def: The mechanism for ingesting log sources -- Microsoft services, third-party products, or custom sources via Azure Monitor Agent with Data Collection Rules, an API, or a diagnostic setting (the legacy Log Analytics agent was retired in August 2024) -- into a Sentinel workspace so its analytics rules and hunting queries have data to run against.
eg: An analytics rule or hunting query referencing a table with no matching connector enabled will simply return no results, which is a common early troubleshooting step.

term: Microsoft Defender portal (security.microsoft.com)
def: The unified console where Defender XDR's correlated incidents, Sentinel (once onboarded to the unified experience), and each individual Defender product's own settings are all managed from one place, instead of separate per-product portals.
eg: The bidirectional sync between Sentinel and Defender XDR incidents is what keeps an incident consistent whether it is worked from this unified portal or from Sentinel's Azure portal experience, which Microsoft plans to retire after March 31, 2027 in favor of the Defender portal.

term: Advanced Security Information Model (ASIM)
def: ASIM normalizes data from many different Sentinel data connectors, each with its own native schema, into a small set of common schemas (like a normalized network session), so one hunting query or analytics rule works across multiple products instead of needing a separate version per source.
prompt: _____ normalizes data from many different Sentinel data connectors, each with its own native schema, into a small set of common schemas (like a normalized network session), so one hunting query or analytics rule works across multiple products instead of needing a separate version per source.
eg: Built-in analytics rules and hunting queries that already use ASIM-normalized fields automatically pick up any new data source once it's mapped to that same normalized schema, with no rule rewrite needed.

term: Built-in Microsoft Sentinel roles: Reader, Responder, Contributor
def: Microsoft Sentinel Reader can view incidents, workbooks, and underlying data but cannot triage or close anything. Responder can additionally manage and triage incidents -- assigning, closing, commenting -- but still cannot create or edit detection content. Contributor goes further still, able to create and edit automation rules, analytics rules, and workbooks, which is the scope actually required to author or tune detections rather than just work incidents that already exist.
eg: A first-line analyst who only needs to view an incident and check an entity's history is over-provisioned with Contributor -- Reader (or Responder, if they also triage) is the scope that actually matches that job, and least-privilege role assignment is graded the same way here as anywhere else in Azure RBAC.

term: Automation rule condition logic: AND vs. OR
def: When an automation rule's conditions are combined with AND, every single condition has to evaluate true before the rule runs at all on a given incident; combined with OR, matching just one condition is enough to trigger it. Getting this backwards is a common reason a rule silently never fires -- a condition set meant to be narrow is easy to mistake for an OR when only a few incidents ever seem to match it.
eg: A rule requiring 'analytics rule name equals X AND account is on the VIP watchlist' does not run at all for a non-VIP account matching that same analytics rule -- the whole rule is skipped, not just the one condition that failed.

term: Microsoft Security analytics rule type
def: The Microsoft Security rule type automatically creates a Sentinel incident from an alert a connected Microsoft security product (such as Defender for Endpoint or Defender for Identity) has already generated, rather than evaluating a custom KQL query the way a scheduled or NRT rule does.
eg: Because it simply mirrors an alert the source product already raised, tuning this rule type means adjusting severity mapping and filters, not writing or troubleshooting KQL the way scheduled and NRT rules require.

term: Sentinel repositories (content as code)
def: Repositories connects a Sentinel workspace to a source-control repository (GitHub or Azure DevOps) so custom analytics rules, hunting queries, and other content are deployed and version-controlled through a CI/CD pipeline instead of being edited directly in the portal -- a different content path from the content hub, which instead installs a vendor-packaged bundle of ready-made content.
eg: Once connected, content edited only in the source repository and merged through a pull request is what actually deploys to the workspace, so hand-editing that same rule back in the portal risks it being overwritten on the next sync.

term: Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) and Data Collection Rules
def: Azure Monitor Agent is the current, unified agent for collecting log and performance data from Windows and Linux machines into a Log Analytics workspace, with exactly what to collect and how to transform it defined by an attached Data Collection Rule -- the same DCR mechanism used for custom log tables -- replacing the older legacy Log Analytics agent (retired in August 2024), which had no equivalent per-machine, rule-driven configuration.
eg: Because AMA's collection scope is entirely defined by its attached DCR rather than fixed per-agent settings, the same installed agent can serve completely different collection needs simply by attaching a different Data Collection Rule.

term: Diagnostic settings
def: A diagnostic setting is what actually routes an Azure resource's own platform logs and metrics -- like Azure Activity Log or a specific resource's audit log -- into a Log Analytics workspace, which is the step that has to exist before Sentinel has anything from that resource to query at all.
eg: This is a different mechanism from a Data Collection Rule feeding Azure Monitor Agent: a diagnostic setting exports an Azure resource's own platform-level logs, while an AMA-based DCR instead governs what's collected from inside a running machine's own operating system.

term: Microsoft Defender for Cloud: Secure Score and regulatory compliance
def: Defender for Cloud continuously assesses Azure (and connected multicloud) resources against security best practices, rolling failed checks up into a single Secure Score and a prioritized list of recommendations -- distinct from an active alert, since a low score on a recommendation is a standing posture gap to remediate, not evidence that an attack has already happened.
eg: The regulatory compliance dashboard reuses those same underlying checks but maps them instead against a specific named standard's control requirements, which is what a security manager reviews to demonstrate conformance to that standard rather than to raw Secure Score.

term: Attack surface reduction (ASR) rules
def: ASR rules in Defender for Endpoint are granular, independently toggleable controls that block specific risky behaviors before they succeed -- such as blocking credential theft from the Windows local security authority subsystem (lsass.exe), blocking Office applications from creating child processes, or blocking execution of potentially obfuscated scripts -- each configurable to block, audit, or warn.
prompt: _____ rules in Defender for Endpoint are granular, independently toggleable controls that block specific risky behaviors before they succeed -- such as blocking credential theft from the Windows local security authority subsystem (lsass.exe), blocking Office applications from creating child processes, or blocking execution of potentially obfuscated scripts -- each configurable to block, audit, or warn.
eg: Because each rule targets one specific technique rather than a broad category, a SOC rolls them out in audit mode first to see what each one would have blocked on real traffic before flipping it to block mode and risking a legitimate workflow breaking.

term: Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management
def: Defender Vulnerability Management gives each onboarded device its own exposure score, built from a continuously updated software and vulnerability inventory, missing security baselines, and prioritized security recommendations -- a device-level, vulnerability-centric posture view distinct from the Secure Score and regulatory compliance views in Microsoft Defender for Cloud, which instead score Azure (and multicloud) resource configuration against best practices.
eg: A security recommendation here is prioritized using the same kind of real-world exploitability and threat context Security Copilot or threat intelligence might also surface, not just a raw CVSS severity number, so the top-ranked item isn't necessarily the highest-severity CVE on paper.

term: Sentinel summary rules
def: A summary rule runs on a schedule to pre-aggregate high-volume raw data (like a running count of sign-ins per user per hour) into a much smaller summary table, so a dashboard or hunting query that only needs the aggregate can scan that small table instead of re-scanning the full raw data every single time it runs.
eg: This is a cost-and-performance optimization layered on top of already-ingested data -- unlike a Data Collection Rule transformation, which reshapes data before it is ever stored, a summary rule pre-computes a reusable aggregate from data already sitting in the workspace.

term: Sentinel SOC optimization
def: SOC optimization analyzes a workspace's own connected data, enabled analytics rules, and ingestion patterns to generate tailored recommendations -- such as a data source with no analytics rule using it, or a table being ingested at high cost with little actual query or detection value -- closing coverage gaps and cutting waste without an analyst having to audit every rule and table by hand.
eg: This complements the MITRE ATT&CK coverage in Sentinel: coverage recommendations point at gaps relative to attacker techniques, while SOC optimization's cost-focused recommendations point at ingestion spend that isn't earning its keep.

term: Microsoft Secure Score vs. Defender for Cloud Secure Score
def: Microsoft Secure Score measures Microsoft 365 identity, device, app, and data posture tenant-wide (things like whether MFA is enforced or mailbox auditing is on), while Defender for Cloud's Secure Score instead scores Azure and connected multicloud resource configuration specifically -- two separately calculated scores covering different resource types, not one combined number.
eg: A tenant can carry a strong Microsoft Secure Score from solid identity hygiene while still showing a weak Defender for Cloud score from unencrypted disks or open management ports, since each score only reflects its own slice of the environment.

term: Defender for Cloud attack path analysis
def: Attack path analysis, a Defender CSPM capability, uses Defender for Cloud's cloud security graph -- a map of resources, their configurations, and how they connect -- to chain together individually low-risk findings (like an internet-exposed VM with a path to a key vault holding sensitive secrets) into a single prioritized path, surfacing which combination is actually exploitable rather than listing every recommendation with equal weight.
eg: This reframes the flat list of recommendations behind Defender for Cloud's Secure Score into a connected risk story -- two recommendations that look equally minor in isolation can matter far more once the graph shows they sit on the same reachable path to a sensitive resource.

term: Scheduled analytics rule settings: query frequency, lookback period, and event grouping
def: A scheduled analytics rule runs its KQL query every set interval and looks back over a set period of data. An alert threshold decides how many results trigger it, and event grouping chooses between one alert summarizing all results or a separate alert for each result.
eg: Keep the lookback at least as long as the run frequency so no events fall between runs. Event grouping controls how many alerts one run produces, not whether alerts merge into an incident.

term: Table plans in Microsoft Sentinel: Analytics, Basic, and Auxiliary
def: Each Log Analytics table in Sentinel has a plan. Analytics gives full KQL, analytics rules and hunting. Basic and Auxiliary cost less per gigabyte but limit queries and features, which makes them suited to high-volume, low-value data such as verbose firewall logs.
eg: Data on a Basic or Auxiliary plan cannot be the source of an analytics rule. If a detection rule depends on a table, that table must stay on the Analytics plan.

term: Microsoft Sentinel data lake
def: The Sentinel data lake is a low-cost tier in the Defender portal for keeping large volumes of security data for up to 12 years. You query it with KQL, jobs and Jupyter notebooks, and jobs can promote useful data to the Analytics tier for detections.
eg: Use it for compliance retention, forensics and large-scale hunting over old data, and keep data you alert on in the Analytics tier. Lake queries are billed by use.

term: Syslog and Common Event Format (CEF) via AMA connectors
def: These Sentinel connectors use the Azure Monitor Agent on a Linux machine to collect Syslog messages, and CEF messages from firewalls and other security appliances, under a data collection rule. The machine can be the source itself or a forwarder for other devices.
prompt: These Sentinel connectors use the Azure Monitor Agent on a Linux machine to collect Syslog messages, and _____ messages from firewalls and other security appliances, under a data collection rule. The machine can be the source itself or a forwarder for other devices.
eg: CEF lands in the CommonSecurityLog table and plain Syslog in the Syslog table. A log forwarder is the usual answer when appliances can only send syslog over the network.

term: Anomaly analytics rules in Microsoft Sentinel
def: Anomaly rules are machine-learning templates tuned by Microsoft that flag unusual behavior and write results to the Anomalies table. They run in a flighting mode for testing and then in production, and you can adjust their thresholds without any machine learning knowledge.
eg: By default anomalies are signals, not alerts or incidents. Use them in hunting queries or as an input to a scheduled rule. UEBA focuses on who behaves oddly, while these rules focus on what activity is odd.

term: Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor role
def: This role is assigned to the Microsoft Sentinel service account on the resource group that holds a playbook, so that automation rules can run it. It is used only for that purpose and is not given to people.
eg: If an automation rule cannot trigger a playbook, check this role assignment on the playbook's resource group. Running playbooks manually also needs Logic App Contributor.

term: Resource-context RBAC and table-level RBAC in Sentinel
def: Resource-context RBAC lets people read logs for Azure resources they already have access to, without access to the whole workspace. Table-level RBAC grants access to specific tables only. Both give narrow data access without the full Sentinel experience.
eg: Use them to let an application team query their own VM logs, or give an auditor one table. Do not give workspace-wide roles when only some data is needed.

term: Microsoft Sentinel in the Defender portal (unified security operations)
def: Microsoft is moving Sentinel into the Microsoft Defender portal, where SIEM data and XDR incidents appear together in one queue. Sentinel in the Azure portal is scheduled to be retired on March 31, 2027, after which it is managed only in the Defender portal.
eg: Exam angle: the same Sentinel features continue, only the portal changes. Connecting a workspace to the Defender portal also brings in the unified incident queue and Defender XDR hunting.

term: Defender for Office 365 preset security policies (Standard and Strict)
def: Preset security policies apply Microsoft's recommended anti-spam, anti-malware, anti-phishing, Safe Links and Safe Attachments settings in one step. Standard suits most users, Strict suits high-value targets, and Built-in protection is the only preset on by default.
eg: Presets are not editable, so use them for fast, consistent protection. Assign Strict to executives and finance, and keep Standard for everyone else.

term: Custom detection rules in Defender XDR
def: A custom detection rule turns an advanced hunting query into a scheduled rule that creates alerts and can take automated response actions on devices, files, users or emails that the query returns. It works across Defender XDR data.
eg: The query must return a timestamp and identifying columns, and for Defender for Endpoint tables that includes DeviceId and ReportId. This is the Defender XDR counterpart to a Sentinel analytics rule.

term: Defender for Cloud plans: Foundational CSPM, Defender CSPM, and workload protection
def: Foundational CSPM is free and covers inventory, recommendations, secure score and compliance. Defender CSPM is a paid plan adding attack path analysis, agentless scanning and a cloud security graph. Workload protection plans, such as Defender for Servers and Storage, add threat detection.
eg: Pick Defender CSPM when the question mentions attack paths. Pick the workload plan for the resource type being attacked, because each plan protects a specific kind of resource.

term: Defender for Cloud Apps: Cloud Discovery
def: Cloud Discovery analyzes firewall and proxy logs, or traffic from Defender for Endpoint devices, against a catalog of cloud apps to show which apps are in use, how risky they are and how many users use them. It is the shadow IT feature.
eg: Admins can mark discovered apps as unsanctioned, and with Defender for Endpoint integration block indicators are created to stop those apps on devices.

term: Windows Security Events via AMA connector
def: This Sentinel connector collects Windows security events from servers and workstations with the Azure Monitor Agent and a data collection rule, and writes them to the SecurityEvent table. You choose a preset, such as All, Common or Minimal, or a custom set of event IDs.
eg: It replaces the legacy agent-based Security Events connector. Choose Minimal or Common to control ingestion cost, and use custom XPath filters to drop noisy event IDs.

term: Email notifications for incidents in Defender XDR
def: Incident notification rules email your staff about new incidents or updates to existing ones. A rule can filter by alert severity, service source (and specific detection source), and device group, and can set a different severity per source, such as Medium and High for endpoint detections but every severity for Defender Experts. You create them in Settings > Microsoft Defender XDR > Email notifications > Incidents tab, and separate notification types exist for response actions and for threat analytics reports.
eg: Configuring notifications needs the Manage security settings permission (or Security Administrator with basic permissions management). With RBAC, you can only manage and receive notifications for the device groups you are allowed to manage.

term: Alert notifications (Defender for Endpoint email rules)
def: Alert notification rules email chosen recipients when new alerts of selected severities appear for selected device groups, with options to include the organization name, a tenant-specific portal link, and device information. They live under Settings > Endpoints > General > Email notifications. Recipients added later only receive alerts triggered after they were added.
eg: With RBAC, users can create, edit, or delete only rules limited to the device groups they manage; only a Global Administrator can manage rules that apply to all device groups.

term: Alert tuning in Defender XDR (previously alert suppression)
def: Alert tuning rules hide or resolve alerts automatically, or convert them to behaviors, when known-benign conditions on the alert's evidence (files, processes, scheduled tasks and so on) are met. Actions are Hide alert (no incident is created, data stays in AlertInfo and AlertEvidence), Resolve alert, and Set as behavior (data stays in BehaviorInfo and BehaviorEntities for hunting). Microsoft also ships built-in alert tuning rules for common benign activity; they do not apply to custom detections or custom threat intelligence alerts.
eg: Create rules under Settings > Microsoft Defender XDR > Alert tuning or from an alert's details page. Built-in rules suppress alerts without stopping automated investigations, and a suppressed alert is reactivated if an investigation finds malicious activity.

term: Alert correlation and analytics rule correlation settings
def: The Defender portal correlates alerts from all sources into incidents and merges incidents as an attack unfolds. For Sentinel analytics rules, you can include or exclude rules from this correlation engine: by default all analytics rules are excluded at the tenant level when you onboard, so incidents are grouped only by each rule's own settings, as they were in Sentinel. You can instead include all rules and exclude specific ones. Managing this needs the Microsoft Sentinel Contributor role.
eg: With several Sentinel workspaces, one is configured as the primary workspace whose alerts can be correlated with Defender alerts.

term: Defender for Endpoint advanced features
def: Settings > Endpoints > Advanced features holds tenant-wide switches, including EDR in block mode (blocks malicious artifacts even when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is passive), automatically resolve alerts, allow or block file, custom network indicators (for IP, domain, and URL indicators, needing network protection), tamper protection, hide potential duplicate device records, and restrict correlation to within scoped device groups.
eg: Custom network indicators and allow or block file are what make indicators of compromise enforceable on devices, so an indicator that does nothing often means the matching advanced feature is still off.

term: Custom data collection in Defender for Endpoint (preview)
def: Custom data collection rules capture endpoint events beyond default telemetry, with filters on properties such as folder paths, process names, and network connections, and store them in a connected Microsoft Sentinel workspace for hunting. They need Defender for Endpoint Plan 2, dynamic tags configured in asset rule management (static tags are not supported), and are limited to one Sentinel workspace per tenant for this feature.
eg: Each rule captures up to 75,000 events per device per rolling 24 hours, after which telemetry for that rule stops until the window resets, so use several focused rules and pilot on a small device group first.

term: Configuring automatic attack disruption
def: Automatic attack disruption is configured by a Global Administrator or Security Administrator and depends on broad deployment of the Defender products, because each detection needs the relevant signals. For Defender for Endpoint, device groups should use the Full remediation level (the recommended setting) and the sensor must meet the minimum version for the Contain user action. You can set exclusions to keep chosen users or devices from being disrupted, and review actions in Incidents and the Action center.
eg: Attack disruption actions for external platforms such as Okta and AWS (preview) additionally need a Sentinel workspace connected to the unified portal with the matching connector.

term: Data tiers and retention: Analytics, Data lake, and XDR default tiers
def: The Analytics tier is hot storage for alerting, hunting, and all Sentinel features, with 30 days of analytics retention by default that can be extended to up to two years. The Data lake tier is low-cost cold storage that supports up to 12 years of total retention, reachable through KQL jobs, notebooks, and summary rules but not real-time detections. Defender XDR tables sit in an XDR default tier with 30 days of analytics retention that can be raised to 90 days with ingestion cost only, and beyond 90 days also incurs storage cost.
eg: By default data in the analytics tier is mirrored to the lake for the same period, so you extend only the total retention to keep it longer. Basic Logs tables can be viewed in the Defender portal but managed only in the Log Analytics workspace unless you change the plan to Analytics.

term: Sentinel roles: Azure roles for the SIEM, Entra roles for the data lake
def: Sentinel SIEM access uses Azure RBAC built-in roles: Reader (view), Responder (also manage incidents), Contributor (also install solutions and create or edit resources), Playbook Operator (run playbooks), and Automation Contributor (lets automation rules run playbooks). The Sentinel data lake instead uses Microsoft Entra roles: Global Reader, Security Reader, Security Operator, and Security Administrator can read across the lake, while Security Operator, Security Administrator, and Global Administrator can write, for example KQL job output to the analytics tier.
eg: Assign the Azure roles at resource group level for best results. Creating or editing playbooks also needs Logic App Contributor, and Responder alone does not let someone create automation rules that call playbooks.

term: SOAR playbook generator (AI-authored playbooks)
def: In the Defender portal, Sentinel customers can describe an automation in natural language and co-author a Python-based playbook with an AI coding agent in an embedded VS Code environment. The result is validated, documented with a flow diagram, and can be tested by supplying a real alert. It does not require a separate Security Copilot license or SCUs.
eg: This complements Logic Apps-based playbooks; automation rules still decide when automation starts.

term: Windows Event Forwarding (WEF) and the Windows Event Collector
def: WEF is a built-in Windows feature in which source computers push chosen events to a central Windows Event Collector (WEC) server through subscriptions. For Sentinel you can install the Azure Monitor Agent on the WEC server and use a data collection rule to send the forwarded events, rather than installing the agent on every source machine, which suits large fleets and servers where an agent is not allowed.
prompt: _____ is a built-in Windows feature in which source computers push chosen events to a central Windows Event Collector (WEC) server through subscriptions. For Sentinel you can install the Azure Monitor Agent on the WEC server and use a data collection rule to send the forwarded events, rather than installing the agent on every source machine, which suits large fleets and servers where an agent is not allowed.
eg: Contrast with the Windows Security Events via AMA connector, where the agent runs on each machine and a DCR picks the event sets or XPath filters to collect.

term: Collecting Azure activity and resource logs with Azure Policy
def: The Azure Activity connector streams subscription-level control-plane events into the AzureActivity table. Azure resource connectors stream resource diagnostic logs by using Azure Policy to apply one log-streaming (diagnostic setting) configuration to all current and future resources of a type within a scope, which needs the Owner role on the policy assignment scope. Resource diagnostic logs usually land in AzureDiagnostics or resource-specific tables.
eg: Without Policy you would create a diagnostic setting by hand on every resource; Policy also remediates new resources automatically. These connectors do not support DCR transformations.

term: KQL jobs in the Sentinel data lake
def: KQL jobs run one-time or scheduled asynchronous queries on data lake tables and federated tables (such as Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft 365, and Resource Graph data) and are suited to long investigations, historical threat intelligence matching, and joins or unions across many tables. A job can promote results to the analytics tier as a new table (named with a _KQL_CL suffix) or append to an existing one, so you can then hunt and alert on it.
eg: Promote only the columns and rows you need because analytics-tier storage costs more than the lake. Use KQL jobs for up to 12 years of data, summary rules for frequent summarization (for example every 20 minutes), and search jobs for archived data or hydrating one big table.

term: Summary rule tables (updated detail)
def: Summary rules aggregate high-volume data on a schedule into custom summary tables in the analytics tier, so dashboards, hunting, and detections query a small table. They can read from Analytics, Auxiliary, Basic, and data lake tables (but not System tables), run as often as every 20 minutes, and have out-of-the-box templates.
eg: They suit workspaces not onboarded to the data lake, such as when the source is on a Basic or Auxiliary plan.

term: Security Copilot agents in the Defender portal
def: Security Copilot agents automate SOC tasks and are deployed from Security Copilot > Security Store in the Defender portal, then set up from Security Copilot > Agents. In Defender they include the Phishing Triage Agent (extended as the Security Alert Triage Agent), the Threat Intelligence Briefing Agent, the Security Analyst Agent, the Dynamic Threat Detection Agent, and the Threat Hunting Assistant. Agents consume Security Compute Units (SCUs) and authenticate with a dedicated Microsoft Entra Agent ID agent identity or a connected user account.
eg: Eligible Microsoft 365 E5 and E7 customers receive Security Copilot with 400 SCUs per month for every 1,000 paid user licenses, up to 10,000 SCUs per month, at no additional cost.

term: Sentinel MCP server
def: Microsoft Sentinel's Model Context Protocol (MCP) support is a hosted, Entra-authenticated server offering scenario-focused tool collections, so AI clients and agents can query Sentinel data lake and Defender data in natural language without knowing table schemas or writing KQL. Compatible hosts include Visual Studio Code, Security Copilot, Copilot Studio, and other MCP-capable AI clients.
eg: In MCP terms the AI application is the host, it runs an MCP client per connection, and the Sentinel server provides the tools. It needs no infrastructure deployment from you.

term: Case management in the Defender portal
def: Case management manages SecOps work natively in the Defender portal. Incident cases (preview, and the recommended experience for incidents) are created from correlated incident activity and track ownership, severity, status, classification, tasks, comments, activity history, custom fields, and resolution. Generic cases are created manually for other SecOps work. Case templates configure custom fields and SLA policies.
eg: Incident case access uses the unified RBAC permissions Security Data Read (view) and Security Data Manage (view and manage), the same model as the legacy incident experience, which remains available during preview.

term: Defender for Endpoint device isolation
def: Device isolation disconnects a compromised endpoint from the network while keeping it connected to Defender for Endpoint, so an analyst can continue investigating and running response actions (like a live response session) on it while it can no longer communicate with other systems or exfiltrate data.
eg: Full isolation cuts nearly all network communication except to the Defender for Endpoint service itself, while selective isolation also leaves Outlook and Teams (and, in older setups, Skype for Business) connected. Where the newer isolation exclusions feature is enabled, admins define their own process, IP, or service exclusions instead, which helps when a business-critical service on that host cannot simply be cut off.

term: Defender for Endpoint live response
def: Live response gives an analyst a remote, real-time command-line session on a device to run scripts, collect forensic artifacts, view and kill processes, or delete files directly, without waiting for a scheduled scan or a full automated investigation.
eg: Live response is the hands-on investigative tool for a specific device once it is already flagged, distinct from automated investigation, which runs its playbook without an analyst driving each command.

term: Defender for Endpoint Action Center: pending vs. completed actions
def: Remediation actions taken by automated investigation (or manually by an analyst) -- like quarantining a file, stopping a process, or isolating a device -- appear in the unified Action Center, where a pending action awaiting approval can be approved or rejected, and a completed action can, where supported, be undone.
eg: Approving a pending action from automated investigation lets remediation proceed exactly as AIR determined; rejecting it stops that specific remediation without undoing any other actions already taken on the same investigation.

term: Indicators of compromise (IOCs) in Defender for Endpoint
def: An administrator can add custom indicators -- file hashes, IP addresses, URLs/domains, or certificates -- and set the action taken when one is seen (allow, audit, warn, or block and remediate), letting the SOC pre-emptively block or flag a known-bad artifact across all onboarded devices.
eg: A file-hash indicator set to block and remediate will stop that specific file from running on every onboarded device tenant-wide, which is a faster, broader response than isolating devices one at a time after each individual detection.

term: Defender for Office 365: Threat Explorer
def: Threat Explorer (Explorer) lets an analyst search and filter email, URL, and file events across the tenant -- by sender, recipient, subject, malware family, or delivery action -- to scope how widely a phishing or malware campaign actually spread before taking remediation action.
eg: Threat Explorer is also where an analyst launches a remediation action (like soft-deleting or moving matching messages) directly from the search results, rather than acting on each mailbox individually.

term: Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) in Defender for Office 365
def: ZAP retroactively detects and neutralizes a malicious or spam message that already reached a mailbox, moving it to Junk Email or Quarantine after delivery, once a threat is confirmed post-delivery through updated detection signatures.
prompt: _____ retroactively detects and neutralizes a malicious or spam message that already reached a mailbox, moving it to Junk Email or Quarantine after delivery, once a threat is confirmed post-delivery through updated detection signatures.
eg: ZAP exists precisely because a message can look clean at time of delivery but be reclassified as malicious minutes or hours later -- without it, that already-delivered message would sit untouched in the inbox indefinitely.

term: Defender for Identity: lateral movement paths
def: Defender for Identity maps lateral movement paths -- the chain of computers and accounts an attacker could hop through, often via cached credentials, to eventually reach a sensitive or highly privileged account -- surfacing that risk before any actual attack occurs.
eg: A lateral movement path is a proactive exposure finding, not an alert about an attack already in progress; it tells a responder which low-privilege compromise would be most dangerous to leave unaddressed, given what it could reach.

term: Defender for Identity: honeytoken accounts
def: A honeytoken account is a decoy account, deliberately left unused in normal operations, configured in Defender for Identity so that any authentication attempt against it is treated as a high-confidence signal of malicious reconnaissance or credential-stuffing activity.
eg: Because a legitimate user or service has no reason to ever authenticate as the honeytoken, essentially any activity on it can be treated as true positive, unlike alerts on real accounts that always carry some chance of legitimate explanation.

term: Defender for Cloud Apps: session policies and Conditional Access App Control
def: Conditional Access App Control routes a user's session through Defender for Cloud Apps as a reverse proxy, letting a session policy enforce real-time controls -- like blocking a download, applying a label, or requiring step-up authentication -- on an already-authenticated session in a sanctioned cloud app.
eg: This is real-time, in-session enforcement, distinct from an access policy that only decides whether the session is allowed to start; a session policy can still act on what a user does after already being let in.

term: Defender for Cloud Apps: anomaly detection policies
def: Built-in anomaly detection policies (impossible travel, activity from an infrequent country, mass download, ransomware activity, and more) run automatically once an app is connected, generating alerts on unusual patterns without an analyst having to author custom detection logic first.
eg: These policies establish their own behavioral baseline per user automatically, similar in spirit to UEBA in Sentinel, so a new anomaly type can surface even without a pre-written rule matching that specific pattern.

term: Automatic attack disruption in Defender XDR
def: Attack disruption uses high-confidence signals correlated across Defender XDR products to automatically contain an in-progress attack -- such as disabling a compromised user account or containing a compromised device -- at machine speed, before a human analyst has necessarily even triaged the incident.
eg: Disruption is deliberately reserved for very high-confidence, fast-moving attack patterns (like human-operated ransomware) specifically because the goal is containing damage in the minutes before an analyst could realistically respond manually.

term: Sentinel incident management: status, severity, and assignment
def: A Sentinel incident moves through statuses (New, Active, Closed) and carries an editable severity, owner assignment, and classification reason (such as True Positive or False Positive) when closed, giving a consistent audit trail of how it was triaged and resolved.
eg: Choosing an accurate closing classification (like 'Undetermined' versus 'False Positive - Incorrect Alert Logic') is what feeds back into tuning which analytics rules or thresholds need adjustment, not just a formality for closing the case.

term: Bidirectional sync between Sentinel and Defender XDR incidents
def: An incident correlated in Defender XDR that includes a Sentinel-connected data source can sync into Sentinel's incident queue, and changes to status, severity, or comments made in either portal are reflected in the other, so an analyst does not have to update the same incident twice.
eg: Working the incident from either portal keeps both in sync -- but closing or reassigning it in Sentinel updates the same incident in Defender XDR moments later, rather than creating a separate, disconnected record.

term: False-positive triage: alert suppression vs. tuning the source signal
def: When an analyst confirms a recurring alert is a genuine false positive caused by known-benign activity (like a vulnerability scanner or an approved automation account), the durable fix is tuning the underlying detection -- excluding that specific entity in the analytics rule query, or adjusting the source product's own alert threshold -- rather than repeatedly closing each new incident it generates by hand.
eg: Manually closing the same false-positive pattern incident after incident does not reduce SOC workload going forward; only a change to the query, indicator, or upstream detection logic itself stops it from recurring.

term: Incident severity vs. entity risk score
def: An incident's severity (Informational through High) reflects how serious the underlying detection is. A separate entity-level score driven by UEBA (the entity's investigation priority) reflects how anomalous a specific user or device's behavior has been over time -- a High-severity incident can involve a normally low-risk user, and vice versa.
eg: Status, severity, and assignment cover the triage workflow; the entity score is one extra signal that helps decide how urgently to act on a given incident.

term: Incident tasks in Sentinel
def: Incident tasks are a checklist of investigation or containment steps — such as running Defender for Endpoint device isolation or notifying the user — attached directly to an incident, either added manually or auto-populated from a template, so every analyst follows the same triage steps regardless of who picks it up.
eg: Tasks are tracked as part of the incident's own record, not a separate ticketing system — completing them updates the incident's audit trail directly.

term: Investigation graph in Sentinel
def: The investigation graph is an interactive, visual map of an incident's related entities (users, hosts, IPs, files) and how they connect, letting an analyst pivot outward from one alert to see the full blast radius instead of reading a flat list of raw events.
eg: A bookmark created during threat hunting can be pulled directly into an investigation graph, connecting ad-hoc hunting findings to a live incident's existing entity map.

term: Safe Attachments Dynamic Delivery
def: Dynamic Delivery lets a recipient read an email's message body immediately while its attachment continues to be scanned in the background by Safe Attachments, swapping in the real file once scanning clears it -- a different timing model than Zero-hour auto purge in Defender for Office 365, which instead acts retroactively on a message that has already been delivered and already looked clean at the time.
eg: Dynamic Delivery removes the tradeoff between blocking the whole message until scanning finishes and letting a user open a still-unscanned attachment immediately -- the body is available right away, but the attachment itself only becomes available once it's actually been cleared.

term: Just-in-time (JIT) VM access
def: Just-in-time VM access in Defender for Cloud locks down a virtual machine's management ports (like RDP or SSH) by default, opening them only for a limited time window and a specific requester's IP address once explicitly requested and approved, shrinking the attack surface those ports would otherwise expose around the clock.
prompt: _____ in Defender for Cloud locks down a virtual machine's management ports (like RDP or SSH) by default, opening them only for a limited time window and a specific requester's IP address once explicitly requested and approved, shrinking the attack surface those ports would otherwise expose around the clock.
eg: This is a preventive, exposure-reduction control rather than a response action taken on an incident already in progress -- it's evaluated well before Defender for Cloud workload protection alerts would have anything to fire on for that same port.

term: Defender for Cloud workload protection alerts
def: Defender for Cloud's workload protection plans (Defender for Servers, Defender for Storage, Defender for SQL, and others) generate alerts on suspicious activity inside those specific Azure or hybrid resources -- like an unusual process on a VM or anomalous access to a storage account -- which surface in the same unified incident queue as Defender XDR and Sentinel once connected, rather than living in a separate, unrelated console.
eg: This is a different signal from just-in-time VM access: JIT reduces standing exposure before anything happens, while a workload protection alert reflects activity Defender for Cloud actually observed and considered suspicious.

term: Safe Links in Defender for Office 365
def: Safe Links rewrites URLs inside email and Office documents so that each click is checked against current threat intelligence at the moment the link is actually clicked, rather than only at the time the message was delivered, blocking a link that was benign at delivery but has since been weaponized.
eg: This click-time check is a different timing model from Safe Attachments Dynamic Delivery, which instead scans a file attachment in the background while still delivering the message body immediately.

term: Microsoft Entra ID Protection risk-based remediation
def: Identity Protection assigns a user risk level (based on a pattern of risky behavior over time) and a sign-in risk level (based on signals on one specific sign-in), and a risk-based Conditional Access policy can act on either automatically -- for example, requiring a secure password change for elevated user risk, or requiring MFA for elevated sign-in risk -- without an analyst manually intervening on every flagged event.
eg: This automatic, ongoing remediation is separate from an analyst manually revoking a compromised user's active sessions during incident response, which cuts off an already-stolen token directly rather than waiting on a risk policy to catch the next sign-in.

term: Defender for Cloud Apps: app governance
def: App governance surfaces the OAuth permissions a third-party app was granted during user consent (like Mail.Read or Files.ReadWrite.All), flags an app as risky based on its permission scope and observed behavior, and lets an admin review and revoke that app's access directly, without disabling the consenting user's own account.
eg: This addresses a different risk than session policies and Conditional Access App Control, which govern a user's own browser session inside a sanctioned app rather than a separately-consented app's own delegated permissions.

term: Defender for Identity sensor architecture
def: Defender for Identity runs as lightweight sensors on domain controllers, AD FS, and AD CS servers (newer v3.x sensors can be activated on servers already onboarded to Defender for Endpoint, with no separate installation), each monitoring local traffic and Windows events, while a cloud-based component correlates signals across all of them -- which is how it detects on-prem Active Directory attacks such as lateral movement paths or honeytoken account hits without needing a network-wide traffic mirror or SPAN port.
eg: Because the sensor runs directly on the monitored server rather than observing network traffic from outside it, Defender for Identity can see authentication activity even when it never crosses a network segment a traditional network sensor would have had visibility into.

term: Incident evidence in Sentinel
def: The Evidence tab on a Sentinel incident lists every alert, bookmark, file, and related entity tied to the case in one place, giving a flat, reviewable inventory of exactly what has been gathered -- a different view from the investigation graph, which instead visualizes how those same entities connect to each other rather than just listing them.
eg: A bookmark pulled in from a separate hunt lands here as one more piece of evidence on the incident, alongside anything automation or an analyst has already attached, rather than needing to be re-described from scratch.

term: Contain user and Contain device actions in Defender XDR
def: Contain user and Contain device are unified Defender XDR response actions that restrict a suspicious account or unmanaged device just enough to stop it from spreading further -- blocking sign-in or network communication with managed resources -- without going as far as fully disabling the account or fully isolating a managed device through Defender for Endpoint's device isolation action.
eg: These actions exist specifically for the in-between case that automatic attack disruption often reaches for -- an entity confident enough to contain right now, but not yet confirmed enough to warrant the fuller, more disruptive response of a full account disable or complete device isolation.

term: Alert classification and determination in Defender XDR
def: Closing an alert or incident in Defender XDR records both a classification (True positive, False positive, or Informational/expected activity) and a more specific determination within it (such as Malware, Phishing, Compromised account, or Security testing), giving a structured, auditable reason distinct from Sentinel incident management's own status/severity/classification fields on the synced incident.
eg: Consistently picking an accurate determination, not just a classification, is what later analytics on alert quality and tuning priorities actually depend on -- two incidents both marked True positive can still need very different follow-up depending on whether the determination was Malware versus Compromised account.

term: Defender for Endpoint device groups and RBAC
def: Devices are organized into device groups (often by business unit, criticality, or OS), and role-based access control then scopes which analysts can see or act on which groups -- so a first-line analyst can be granted response actions only on a non-critical device group while a senior analyst retains access tenant-wide.
eg: Device group membership can also drive which automated investigation and response (AIR) automation level applies, so a device group holding a company's most sensitive servers can be deliberately left on a Semi level requiring approval even while less sensitive groups run fully automatic remediation.

term: Microsoft Defender for IoT in the SOC
def: Defender for IoT discovers and monitors unmanaged IoT and operational technology (OT) devices -- the kind that cannot run a standard endpoint agent -- passively analyzing network traffic to detect anomalies and vulnerabilities, with its alerts flowing into the same unified Defender XDR incident queue and Sentinel workspace as every other connected product once integrated.
eg: This closes a visibility gap none of the other Defender products address, since Defender for Endpoint's own sensor-based detection assumes a device that can actually run its agent, which most OT and IoT devices simply cannot.

term: Threat analytics in Defender XDR
def: Threat analytics is a set of reports from Microsoft security researchers on specific named threats, such as an active campaign or a new vulnerability. Each report shows related incidents, impacted assets and whether your devices are exposed, with mitigation guidance.
eg: Use it to learn whether a headline threat affects you. It reports on specific threats and exposure, unlike MITRE coverage, which maps your detections to techniques.

term: Collect investigation package (Defender for Endpoint)
def: Collect investigation package is a response action that gathers a fixed set of forensic data from a device into an archive, such as installed programs, autostart entries, running processes, network connections and event logs. It runs no commands on the device.
prompt: _____ is a response action that gathers a fixed set of forensic data from a device into an archive, such as installed programs, autostart entries, running processes, network connections and event logs. It runs no commands on the device.
eg: It fits when you need evidence to analyze offline. If the analyst needs to run scripts or fetch a particular file interactively, use live response instead.

term: Restrict app execution (Defender for Endpoint)
def: Restrict app execution applies a code integrity policy to a Windows device so that only Microsoft-signed apps can run. It limits what an attacker can launch on a compromised machine while the device stays on the network, and it can be removed later.
prompt: _____ applies a code integrity policy to a Windows device so that only Microsoft-signed apps can run. It limits what an attacker can launch on a compromised machine while the device stays on the network, and it can be removed later.
eg: It is milder than full isolation, which cuts network access. Choose it when you want to stop unknown binaries running but keep the device reachable for investigation.

term: Run antivirus scan (Defender for Endpoint response action)
def: Run antivirus scan starts a quick or full Microsoft Defender Antivirus scan on a device from the device page in the Defender portal. The result is recorded in the Action center, and detected threats are handled by the antivirus policy.
prompt: _____ starts a quick or full Microsoft Defender Antivirus scan on a device from the device page in the Defender portal. The result is recorded in the Action center, and detected threats are handled by the antivirus policy.
eg: It is a manual action, so it needs no automation setup. It is available in Plan 1 as well as Plan 2, unlike live response, which needs Plan 2.

term: Stop and quarantine a file (Defender for Endpoint)
def: Stop and quarantine a file ends the processes running a file and moves that file into quarantine on the device, so it can no longer run. The action can be reversed from the Action center if the file turns out to be safe.
prompt: _____ ends the processes running a file and moves that file into quarantine on the device, so it can no longer run. The action can be reversed from the Action center if the file turns out to be safe.
eg: Add an indicator to block a file, by contrast, blocks it across the whole organization. Quarantine handles a file seen in an alert, and an indicator blocks it everywhere.

term: Entity pages in Microsoft Sentinel
def: An entity page collects what Sentinel knows about one entity, such as an account, host, IP address or URL. It shows basic details, a timeline of related alerts, bookmarks and activities, and behavior insights, and can be opened from an incident or by search.
eg: It is the quickest place to answer what else this account or host has been doing. The timeline makes it easy to see related alerts across incidents.

term: Email remediation actions: soft delete vs hard delete
def: In Defender for Office 365, an admin can remediate delivered email by moving it to Inbox, Junk or Deleted Items, or by soft deleting or hard deleting it. Soft delete leaves the message recoverable by the user, while hard delete removes it permanently.
eg: Use soft delete for a likely threat you may need to restore, and hard delete for confirmed malicious mail. Purge actions are limited to messages delivered in roughly the last 30 days.

term: Admin submissions in the Defender portal
def: Admin submissions let a security admin send messages, URLs or files to Microsoft for analysis and say whether they were wrongly blocked, a false positive, or wrongly allowed, a false negative. The verdict can also feed allow or block entries.
eg: Use submissions to report a missed phish so detections improve. It also makes Microsoft's verdict visible, so you can see why a message was or was not blocked.

term: Attack simulation training (Defender for Office 365)
def: Attack simulation training lets an organization run harmless phishing simulations, such as credential harvest or malicious attachment, against its users and assign training to those who fall for them. It needs Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 or Microsoft 365 E5.
prompt: _____ lets an organization run harmless phishing simulations, such as credential harvest or malicious attachment, against its users and assign training to those who fall for them. It needs Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 or Microsoft 365 E5.
eg: It measures and improves user behavior rather than blocking mail. Reports show click and report rates, and payload automation can turn real reported phish into simulations.

term: Pass-the-hash and pass-the-ticket attacks
def: In pass-the-hash, an attacker reuses a captured NTLM password hash to authenticate without knowing the password. In pass-the-ticket, they reuse a stolen Kerberos ticket. Both let them move laterally using credentials taken from memory, and Defender for Identity detects them.
eg: Both are lateral movement techniques that use stolen credentials. Defender for Identity raises alerts such as suspected pass-the-ticket, and lateral movement paths show which accounts make this easy.

term: DCSync attack
def: In a DCSync attack, an attacker with directory replication rights pretends to be a domain controller and asks for password data through the directory replication protocol. This can reveal account hashes, including the krbtgt account. Defender for Identity detects it.
prompt: In a _____, an attacker with directory replication rights pretends to be a domain controller and asks for password data through the directory replication protocol. This can reveal account hashes, including the krbtgt account. Defender for Identity detects it.
eg: Alerts fire when replication is requested by a machine that is not a domain controller. Watch for accounts holding replicating directory changes rights that should not have them.

term: Mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to respond (MTTR)
def: Mean time to detect is the average time from an attack starting to the SOC noticing it. Mean time to respond is the average time from detection to containing or closing the incident. They are the headline measures of how well a SOC performs.
eg: Automation rules, playbooks and tuned analytics rules aim to lower both numbers. Sentinel workbooks that track incident time to triage and time to closure help show whether changes are working.

term: Device timeline in Defender for Endpoint
def: The Timeline tab of a device page shows a chronological view of the events and associated alerts observed on that device, so an analyst can follow a suspected attack step by step. You can filter by event type, review the MITRE ATT&CK techniques linked to events, open process trees, and flag events for follow-up.
eg: The timeline can show activity that is newer than the device page's Last seen value, so trust the timeline when the two disagree.

term: Purview Insider Risk Management and DLP alerts in Defender XDR
def: Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management alerts appear in the Defender portal under Incidents & alerts, can be grouped with DLP and Microsoft Entra ID alerts in one incident, can be filtered by service source, and stay synchronized with Purview. Analysts can hunt for all activity tied to the user in the alert. DLP alerts are handled the same way, with remediation in place on users, files, and devices.
eg: A built-in alert tuning rule for DLP signals took effect in early October 2026: it sets them as behaviors, so they stop generating alerts and incidents but remain in BehaviorInfo and BehaviorEntities. Disable the rule under Settings > Microsoft Defender XDR > Alert tuning to keep DLP alerts.

term: Microsoft Purview Audit (Standard vs. Premium)
def: Purview Audit records user and admin activity in the unified audit log and is enabled by default. Audit (Standard) retains records for 180 days and supports the audit search tool, the Audit Search Graph API, and the Search-UnifiedAuditLog cmdlet. Audit (Premium) includes all of that, keeps records up to one year (ten years with an add-on), and offers audit log retention policies and higher bandwidth access to the Office 365 Management Activity API.
eg: For a business email compromise investigation, audit records of mailbox rule changes and sign-ins from the unified audit log often provide the timeline; if the event is older than the retention window it is gone.

term: Content search in Purview eDiscovery
def: Microsoft Purview eDiscovery lets investigators search Exchange Online mailboxes, SharePoint sites, OneDrive, Teams, Microsoft 365 Groups, and Viva Engage in one search and export results. Classic Content Search, classic eDiscovery (Standard), and classic eDiscovery (Premium) were retired on August 31, 2025 (except for Microsoft 365 operated by 21Vianet); content search features now live in the search experience of the new eDiscovery, including a Content Search case.
eg: Access requires membership in the eDiscovery Manager role group in the Purview portal. Content search finds items in place; it does not itself investigate sign-in or API activity, which come from audit and Graph logs.

term: Microsoft Graph activity logs
def: Microsoft Graph activity logs are an audit trail of every HTTP request the Graph service processes for a tenant, from apps, SDKs, scripts, and Microsoft portals. They are off until a tenant admin enables them with a diagnostic setting that sends them to Log Analytics, storage, or Event Hubs; this needs Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 and Security Administrator is the least privileged supported role. In Log Analytics they appear in the MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs table with fields such as AppId, UserId, ServicePrincipalId, IPAddress, RequestUri, and ResponseStatusCode.
prompt: _____ are an audit trail of every HTTP request the Graph service processes for a tenant, from apps, SDKs, scripts, and Microsoft portals. They are off until a tenant admin enables them with a diagnostic setting that sends them to Log Analytics, storage, or Event Hubs; this needs Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 and Security Administrator is the least privileged supported role. In Log Analytics they appear in the MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs table with fields such as AppId, UserId, ServicePrincipalId, IPAddress, RequestUri, and ResponseStatusCode.
eg: They show what a stolen token or malicious app actually did through the API, such as mass mailbox reads, which sign-in logs alone do not reveal. Advanced hunting has a related GraphAPIAuditEvents table.

term: Investigating incidents with agentic AI
def: Embedded Security Copilot and its agents speed up investigations: the Security Analyst Agent runs ready-made or custom analyses (anomaly detection, clustering, risk scoring) on Defender, Sentinel Log Analytics, or data lake data from a prompt or from Analyze with copilot in advanced hunting; the Threat Hunting Assistant turns natural language into KQL and interprets results; the Dynamic Threat Detection Agent raises alerts for gaps it finds with MITRE-mapped explanations. Incident cases can also run agentic playbooks and show agent session output.
eg: An analyst remains responsible for validating what an agent concludes before acting. Agents consume SCUs and run under an agent identity or a connected user account.

term: Releasing actions taken by automatic attack disruption
def: Containment taken by automatic attack disruption, such as a contained user account or an isolated device, appears in the incident and in the Action center. An analyst reviews the incident evidence, and if the detection is judged a false positive, undoes the action from the Action center so the user or device regains access.
eg: Excluding a device or user from disruption in the configuration is a preventive control; releasing the action in the Action center is the corrective one after the fact.

term: KQL query pipeline basics
def: A KQL query starts from a table, then pipes (|) through operators applied left to right -- where to filter rows, project or extend to shape columns, and summarize to aggregate -- with each operator narrowing or reshaping the result of the one before it.
eg: Operator order matters for both correctness and performance: filtering early with where before an expensive summarize or join reduces the volume every later operator has to process. Every one of these queries ultimately runs against a Log Analytics workspace.

term: Hunting queries vs. analytics rules
def: A hunting query is a KQL query an analyst runs manually to proactively search for evidence of a threat that has not yet triggered any alert, while an analytics rule runs automatically and creates an incident the moment its query condition matches.
eg: A hunting query that keeps turning up a genuine finding is a strong candidate to be promoted into a scheduled analytics rule, so the same pattern is detected automatically going forward instead of relying on an analyst re-running it by hand.

term: Bookmarks in Sentinel hunting
def: A bookmark saves a specific set of interesting hunting-query results, with the original query and any analyst notes attached, so that evidence can be revisited, shared, or later added directly as evidence to a new or existing incident.
eg: Bookmarking is what lets a hunt that turns up real evidence flow directly into a formal incident investigation without an analyst having to manually re-describe or re-run the query later to recreate that evidence.

term: Livestream in Sentinel (retired)
def: Livestream was a Sentinel hunting feature that ran a KQL query interactively and surfaced new matches in near real time during a session. It is no longer available: Microsoft recommends KQL jobs, analytics rules, or playbooks for persistent query results and notifications.
eg: Older material describes livestream as a temporary, session-based watch that was not a saved, recurring detection. The replacement for ongoing alerting is an analytics rule (scheduled or NRT); the replacement for scheduled long-running queries over lake data is a KQL job.

term: KQL join types: inner vs. leftouter
def: An inner join returns only rows with a matching key in both the left and right tables, useful for correlating two data sources where you only care about confirmed matches. A leftouter join returns every row from the left table, filling in nulls for the right side when no match exists, while a leftanti join returns only the left-side rows that have no match at all.
eg: A negative question like 'which watchlisted accounts had zero sign-ins in the last 7 days' is answered directly by leftanti; leftouter also surfaces those accounts but needs an extra filter on the null right-side key, and an inner join would simply drop them from the result.

term: let statements and reusable KQL functions
def: A let statement assigns a scalar value, a list, or an entire tabular query to a named variable within a query, and a saved function (built from a let statement referencing a query) lets that same reusable logic be called by name across many different hunting queries or analytics rules.
eg: Defining a watchlist of suspicious process names once as a let statement, then referencing that variable in several downstream where clauses, keeps the list consistent and avoids retyping (and potentially mistyping) it in every query that needs it.

term: Advanced hunting across Defender XDR (M365D schema)
def: Defender XDR's advanced hunting exposes a shared set of KQL-queryable tables across products -- DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceNetworkEvents from Defender for Endpoint, EmailEvents from Defender for Office 365, IdentityLogonEvents from Defender for Identity, and CloudAppEvents from Defender for Cloud Apps -- letting one query correlate activity across all of them.
eg: A single hunting query can join DeviceProcessEvents to EmailEvents on a shared device or user identifier to trace a suspicious process directly back to the phishing email that likely delivered it, without switching between separate per-product consoles.

term: Hunting across Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft Purview data
def: Sentinel and Defender XDR advanced hunting can also query Microsoft Entra ID sign-in and audit logs (SigninLogs, AuditLogs) and Microsoft Purview audit data once those sources are connected, letting a hunt correlate an endpoint or email finding with identity sign-in patterns or a sensitive data-access/exfiltration event.
eg: Correlating a suspicious mailbox rule change in Purview audit data with an unusual sign-in in SigninLogs for the same account is a classic hunt for confirming business email compromise, since either signal alone might otherwise be dismissed as routine.

term: Cyber kill chain
def: A model describing the sequential stages of an attack — reconnaissance, initial access, execution, persistence, lateral movement, and exfiltration/impact — used to reason about how far an intrusion has progressed and what to look for at each stage.
eg: MITRE ATT&CK coverage in Sentinel maps specific attacker techniques onto roughly this same progression, giving each analytics rule a stage in the chain it's meant to detect.

term: has vs. contains vs. == in KQL string matching
def: has matches whole terms from a pre-built term index and is the fastest option for finding a specific token in a string column; contains performs a slower substring scan that also matches inside a larger word; == requires an exact, full-string match with no partial matching at all.
eg: Reaching for has instead of contains when searching for a specific complete word, like a process name, in a where clause is a common hunting-query performance optimization, since contains has to scan every character position rather than checking indexed whole terms.

term: mv-expand operator
