def: mv-expand takes a single row containing a dynamic array or property bag column and expands it into one row per element, which is what lets a hunting query filter, join, or summarize individual values buried inside a JSON-like column instead of treating the whole array as one opaque value.
eg: A raw log row with a dynamic array of several file hashes attached to one event, for example, only becomes queryable hash by hash after mv-expand splits that array out into its own row per hash.

term: parse operator
def: parse extracts one or more named fields out of an unstructured string column by matching it against a specified pattern, turning a single free-text column -- like a raw command-line string -- into separate, individually queryable fields without needing a Data Collection Rule transformation or a custom parser built ahead of time.
eg: This is useful precisely when the data needed for a hunt was never given its own column at ingestion time, letting an analyst pull it out ad hoc within the hunting query itself instead of re-ingesting the source data differently.

term: Jupyter notebooks in Microsoft Sentinel
def: Sentinel notebooks run in an attached Azure Machine Learning workspace and let an analyst combine KQL queries with full Python code -- calling machine learning libraries, external threat intelligence APIs, or custom visualizations -- for hunting scenarios too complex for KQL alone, such as clustering related entities or scoring anomalies with a custom model. Notebooks over the Sentinel data lake instead run through the Microsoft Sentinel extension for Visual Studio Code using PySpark on Spark compute.
eg: This goes further than a saved hunting query, which is still fundamentally a single-KQL-query tool with no general-purpose programming language layered on top.

term: Search jobs and restoring archived logs
def: A search job runs an asynchronous query across data on the low-cost Basic Logs table plan or Archive tier and writes matching rows into a new search-results table (suffixed _SRCH) that is queryable like any other table, while restoring a specific time range from Archive tier instead creates a restored table (suffixed _RST) for that whole range, queryable until it is deleted, without waiting on a job to filter results.
eg: Both exist because Basic Logs and Archive-tier data are deliberately not directly queryable at full interactive speed the way standard Analytics-tier data in a Log Analytics workspace is, so a genuine long-range hunt over that older, cheaper data has to explicitly bring it back within reach first.

term: union operator in KQL
def: union combines rows from two or more tables with a similar or overlapping schema into one result set, stacking them vertically -- a different operation from a join type like inner or leftouter, which instead combines columns from two tables side by side by matching on a key.
eg: A hunting query that needs every event of several related kinds -- say, union DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceNetworkEvents -- to look for a pattern spanning both reaches for union specifically because neither table alone has every row the hunt needs, and there's no shared key to join them on in the first place.

term: bag_unpack operator in KQL
def: bag_unpack expands a single dynamic property bag column (key-value pairs, like a JSON object) into one column per key, which is the property-bag counterpart to mv-expand, which instead expands a dynamic array into one row per element.
eg: A raw event with a single AdditionalFields column holding several named properties only becomes queryable field by field, each in its own column, after bag_unpack splits that property bag out -- compare that to a column holding an array of several values, which calls for mv-expand instead.

term: Cross-workspace KQL queries
def: The workspace() function lets a KQL query in one Log Analytics workspace reach into a table in a different workspace -- and resource() does the same for a specific Azure resource's own logs -- letting a hunt correlate data that a larger organization has deliberately split across multiple separate Sentinel workspaces (often by subscription, region, or business unit).
eg: This matters specifically because entity mapping, alert grouping, and most KQL pipelines otherwise assume all the needed data already lives in one workspace -- without workspace(), a hunt split across workspace boundaries would have to be run and manually reconciled separately in each one.

term: KQL aggregation functions: count(), dcount(), and arg_max()
def: Used with summarize, count() totals all rows, dcount() returns the approximate number of distinct values, and arg_max() returns the full row with the highest value of a column. Together they turn raw events into per-user or per-device summaries.
eg: dcount(IPAddress) by user finds users signing in from many addresses, while count() would only total sign-ins. arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) keeps the latest row and all its columns.

term: KQL bin() and ago() functions
def: ago() returns a point in time a given distance in the past, such as ago(7d), and is used to filter by recent time. bin() rounds values down to a fixed size, so summarize by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) buckets events into hourly groups.
eg: Combine them to count events per hour over the last day. Narrow the time range first with ago(), because it makes the query faster and cheaper.

term: KQL make-series and series_decompose_anomalies
def: make-series builds a regular time series, with a value for every time slot, and series_decompose_anomalies() flags points that break the normal trend or seasonal pattern. It is how a hunter finds unusual spikes without picking a fixed threshold.
eg: Typical use: build an hourly count of sign-ins or data uploads, then flag the hour that deviates from the baseline. Results are arrays, so mv-expand or render timechart makes them readable.

term: KQL externaldata and datatable operators
def: datatable defines a small table inline in the query, and externaldata reads a table from a file at a URL, such as a list of bad IP addresses in a storage account. Both let a query use a custom list without ingesting it first.
eg: Use datatable for a short allow or block list typed into the query, and externaldata for a larger list that someone else maintains. A Sentinel watchlist is the managed alternative.

term: KQL parse_json() and dynamic columns
def: parse_json() converts a JSON string into a dynamic value that the query can read by property name, as in AdditionalFields.ProcessName. todynamic() does the same, and the resulting properties can then be filtered, projected and summarized.
eg: Many security tables store details as a string of JSON. Without parsing it you can only search the whole text, while parsing lets you filter on one field.

term: KQL regex: extract() and matches regex
def: extract() pulls the text matched by a regular expression capture group out of a string, and the matches regex operator filters rows whose text matches a pattern. They help when the value you need is buried inside a longer string.
eg: Use extract() to take a domain from a URL or a user from a log line. Regex is slower than has or ==, so use it only after cheaper filters have reduced the rows.

term: SecurityAlert and SecurityIncident tables
def: In a Sentinel workspace, SecurityAlert holds alerts from analytics rules and connected Microsoft security products, and SecurityIncident holds incidents with their status, owner and classification. Both can be queried with KQL to report on or hunt through alerts.
eg: SecurityIncident writes a new row each time an incident changes, so use arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by IncidentNumber to see the latest state of each incident.

term: CommonSecurityLog and Syslog tables
def: CommonSecurityLog stores Common Event Format messages from firewalls, proxies and other security appliances, and Syslog stores standard Linux and network device syslog messages. They are the main tables for network device and Linux hunting in Sentinel.
eg: Firewall allow and deny events, and many Linux logins, are found here. If a hunt needs network device logs, check these tables first.

term: OfficeActivity table
def: OfficeActivity holds Microsoft 365 audit activity from Exchange Online, SharePoint Online and Teams, collected through the Microsoft 365 connector in Sentinel. It records actions such as file downloads, mailbox rule creation and sharing.
eg: A hunter looking for suspicious mailbox forwarding rules or mass file downloads queries this table. It complements sign-in logs by showing what a user did after authenticating.

term: Hunts in Microsoft Sentinel
def: The Hunts feature in Sentinel organizes proactive threat hunting around a hypothesis. It groups related queries and bookmarks, records whether the hypothesis was validated, and lets the hunter turn findings into analytics rules, threat indicators or incidents.
eg: It is the structured, trackable way to hunt. A saved query alone shows results, but a hunt keeps the evidence, notes and outcome together.

term: AlertInfo and AlertEvidence tables (advanced hunting)
def: In Defender XDR advanced hunting, AlertInfo holds alert details such as title, severity and category, and AlertEvidence holds the files, IP addresses, URLs, users and devices tied to each alert. Both share an AlertId column for joining.
eg: Join them on AlertId to list every entity involved in an alert. They cover alerts from all Defender workloads, and they replace the older device-only alerts table.

term: Hunting graph in Defender XDR
def: The hunting graph renders threat scenarios in advanced hunting as an interactive graph of entities and relationships, so an analyst can trace paths and possible choke points and take actions on results that tabular KQL output might hide. Open it from Investigation & response > Hunting > Advanced hunting using the hunting graph icon. It depends on the Microsoft Sentinel data lake and at least read-only access to Microsoft Security Exposure Management.
eg: Use it to see how entities connect (for example a user with privileged access paths to a critical asset), instead of joining many tables by hand.

term: Blast radius analysis in the incident graph
def: Blast radius analysis extends the incident graph in Defender to show the vulnerable paths an attacker could take from a compromised entity to a critical asset, so one consolidated graph shows the current impact of a breach and the possible future impact. It is powered by Microsoft Sentinel graph and is auto-provisioned when you already have the Sentinel data lake.
eg: Blast radius is about what could happen next; the hunting graph is the analyst-driven exploration tool. Purview Insider Risk Management has a similar data risk graph for data leak blast radius.

term: Microsoft Sentinel graph and custom graphs
def: Microsoft Sentinel graph models assets, identities, activities, and threat intelligence as nodes and edges, answering questions such as what the blast radius of a compromised account or document is. Custom graphs (preview) are authored in a Jupyter notebook with the Microsoft Sentinel extension for Visual Studio Code, published and materialized by a graph job, and queried with Graph Query Language (GQL) on the Graphs page in the Defender portal.
eg: On-demand graph jobs keep a graph for 30 days, while scheduled graph jobs rebuild it on your refresh schedule. Usage is billed under the Sentinel graph meter.

term: EntraIdSignInEvents (replaces AADSignInEventsBeta)
def: EntraIdSignInEvents is the advanced hunting table for Microsoft Entra interactive and non-interactive sign-ins, and EntraIdSpnSignInEvents covers service principal and managed identity sign-ins. The AADSignInEventsBeta table was deprecated on October 19, 2026, and queries that used it were migrated automatically to EntraIdSignInEvents.
prompt: _____ is the advanced hunting table for Microsoft Entra interactive and non-interactive sign-ins, and EntraIdSpnSignInEvents covers service principal and managed identity sign-ins. The AADSignInEventsBeta table was deprecated on October 19, 2026, and queries that used it were migrated automatically to _____.
eg: In a Sentinel workspace the equivalent tables are SigninLogs and the non-interactive and service principal sign-in log tables; the Entra-prefixed tables are the Defender XDR advanced hunting names.

term: Choosing the right advanced hunting table
def: Match the question to the table: UrlClickEvents for Safe Links clicks from email, Teams, and Office apps; EmailEvents, EmailAttachmentInfo, and EmailUrlInfo for messages, attachments, and URLs; DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceFileEvents, DeviceNetworkEvents, and DeviceLogonEvents for endpoint activity; IdentityLogonEvents and IdentityQueryEvents for Active Directory authentication and directory queries; CloudAppEvents for cloud app activity; GraphAPIAuditEvents for Microsoft Graph API requests; AlertInfo and AlertEvidence for alerts.
eg: When a case needs both a click and its landing activity, join UrlClickEvents to DeviceNetworkEvents or EmailUrlInfo on the URL or user instead of searching one table broadly.

term: Hunting with notebooks on the data lake and the Sentinel MCP server
def: Notebooks over the Sentinel data lake are Jupyter notebooks run through the Microsoft Sentinel extension for Visual Studio Code using PySpark on Spark compute, suited to low-and-slow attack detection, anomaly and machine learning analysis, and visualization across large data. An MCP client such as VS Code can additionally connect to the Sentinel MCP server so an AI assistant can query the same lake data in natural language.
eg: Notebook jobs can be scheduled, and you can promote findings to the analytics tier with a KQL job for alerting.

term: KQL jobs vs. summary rules vs. search jobs (when to hunt with which)
def: Use a KQL job for up to 12 years of lake data with full KQL, joins, and unions, one-time or scheduled. Use a summary rule for frequent aggregation (as often as every 20 minutes) of Analytics, Basic, Auxiliary, or lake data into analytics-tier summary tables. Use a search job for data in the archive tier (or older than your data lake onboarding date) and to hydrate a large volume from a single table into a new table.
eg: If the question mentions joins across many tables over years, think KQL job; frequent small aggregates, summary rule; archived or one-table forensic retrieval, search job.
